clinicalPearls: The commonest radiologically identifiable inner-ear malformation associated with paediatric sensorineural hearing loss
Diagnosis rests on cross-sectional imaging showing a vestibular aqueduct that exceeds accepted midpoint or opercular diameter thresholds
Hearing loss is characteristically fluctuating and stepwise progressive, sometimes worsening after minor head trauma or barotrauma
Frequently associated with biallelic or monoallelic SLC26A4 (pendrin) variants, placing it on a spectrum with Pendred syndrome
A low-frequency air-bone gap can appear despite a sensorineural lesion, reflecting a third-window effect rather than middle-ear disease
Often bilateral and may coexist with cochlear incomplete partition on imaging
Counselling should include avoidance of contact sports and heavy straining that may precipitate sudden drops in hearing
reference.pathophysiology: The vestibular aqueduct is a bony canal transmitting the endolymphatic duct and sac. When abnormally enlarged, the endolymphatic system is dysregulated, and it is thought that transmission of cerebrospinal-fluid or intracranial pressure changes and reflux of hyperosmolar endolymphatic sac contents toward the cochlea injure hair cells, producing fluctuating and progressive sensorineural loss. Many cases arise from variants in SLC26A4, which encodes pendrin, an anion transporter important for endolymph ion and pH homeostasis; when Pendred syndrome coexists there is additional thyroid dyshormonogenesis. The dilated aqueduct also creates an abnormal mobile communication that behaves as a third window, contributing to a low-frequency conductive appearance.
additionalDifferentials: Pendred syndrome with goitre and organification defect
Otosclerosis producing a genuine conductive or mixed loss
Superior semicircular canal dehiscence and other third-window lesions
Cochlear incomplete partition without aqueduct enlargement
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution temporal bone imaging to measure the vestibular aqueduct and assess cochleovestibular anatomy
Serial pure-tone audiometry to document fluctuation and progression
Tympanometry and otoacoustic emissions to distinguish third-window effects from middle-ear disease
SLC26A4 genetic testing and wider deafness panel where indicated
Thyroid assessment and perchlorate discharge or equivalent testing when Pendred syndrome is suspected
Vestibular testing when balance symptoms are present
redFlags: Sudden or stepwise hearing drop following head trauma, straining, or barotrauma
Rapid bilateral progression threatening useful hearing
New vestibular symptoms suggesting endolymphatic decompensation
Features of Pendred syndrome such as goitre requiring endocrine review
reference.prognosis: Hearing tends to fluctuate and decline over years, sometimes to severe or profound levels; protective counselling may slow drops, and cochlear implantation gives good results when hearing aids no longer suffice.
pitfalls: Misreading the low-frequency air-bone gap as middle-ear disease and pursuing unnecessary ear surgery
Failing to counsel against activities that risk sudden hearing loss
Not testing for SLC26A4 variants or overlooking coexisting Pendred syndrome
Assuming stability and omitting serial audiometry
references: GeneReviews: Pendred Syndrome / DFNB4 and SLC26A4-Related Hearing Loss
management: No specific medical cure exists; management centres on hearing preservation, amplification and counselling
Counsel on protective measures to avoid head trauma and barotrauma, advising against contact sports and scuba diving that can precipitate stepwise hearing loss
Fit and optimise hearing aids for the fluctuating and progressive sensorineural loss, with serial audiometry
Proceed to cochlear implantation when hearing loss progresses beyond benefit from hearing aids, which gives good results
Consider a trial of corticosteroids for acute hearing drops, recognising the limited evidence
Assess and manage associated Pendred syndrome, including thyroid function and goitre
Offer SLC26A4 genetic testing and counselling, screen for associated inner-ear malformations, and provide educational and speech-language support
